posts.title: Muxer: check coding sessions from Android
posts.promise: A private-network way to view and respond to cmux sessions on your phone.
posts.whatItIs: Muxer pairs an Android app with a computer relay. Its README describes viewing cmux workspaces and terminals, replying, and receiving notifications over a private network.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: an individual developer who uses cmux might pay for convenient phone access; the source establishes no buyers or pricing.
loop: Install cmux and Muxer on compatible devices.
Set the relay to use cmux’s local control socket.
Put the relay behind HTTPS access limited to your devices.
Pair the phone using a one-time code.
Review a session or notification and send a reply only when intended.
posts.evidence: The GitHub README documents the Android app, relay, pairing flow, notifications, and terminal controls.
posts.uncertainty: This is maker documentation, not independent user evidence. Setup requires a computer, compatible cmux, Android, and private HTTPS access. The app can read terminals and type into cmux, so a person must control pairing and review every action; no AI operator is evidenced.
first24Hours: Read the README setup and security sections.
Sketch a test with a spare computer and phone on a private network.
Pair and verify a harmless test message; a visible session and correctly delivered reply would show whether the documented task works.

ease.reason: README gives install and pairing steps, but setup needs cmux, Android, and private HTTPS.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: cmux users may value phone access; the source gives no buyer or pricing evidence.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test can pair devices and check sessions, but requires compatible equipment and network setup.

autonomy.reason: Relay streams terminal updates and notifications; a person must pair devices and choose replies.

evidence.reason: The repository README documents app features and a working setup, without independent use evidence.

posts.title: n8n: prototype a bounded AI workflow
posts.promise: Test one scheduled workflow with visible steps and human approval for risky actions.
posts.whatItIs: n8n describes workflows triggered by schedules, webhooks, or events, and agents using tools within defined limits. It also describes logs, test runs, and human approval steps.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small team already using n8n might pay for setup help; the source provides no customer or pricing evidence.
loop: Choose one low-risk repetitive task and define its input and output.
Build a workflow from explicit steps and connect only needed tools.
Add an AI step only where a judgment call is needed.
Set limits and require human approval before consequential actions.
Test runs, inspect inputs and outputs, and review execution history.
posts.evidence: The n8n product page describes triggered workflows, test runs, execution logs, tool limits, and human approvals.
posts.uncertainty: This is product-page evidence, not proof of customer demand or outcomes. Setup depends on integrations and permissions. Automation can execute configured steps; people must validate outputs and approve consequential actions.
first24Hours: Read n8n’s workflow and human-approval descriptions.
Write down one task with a harmless sample input and expected output.
Map the workflow and approval point; a completed test run with a human-confirmed result would show whether the proposed task is handled.

ease.reason: The page offers a natural-language assistant and templates, while a useful test still needs tool configuration.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: teams may pay for setup help, but the page establishes no demand or pricing.

feasibility.reason: A narrow four-week workflow test is plausible, though integration and permission setup depend on the task.

autonomy.reason: Triggers and workflow steps can run automatically; limits and human approval remain necessary.

evidence.reason: The product page documents workflows, agents, testing, logs, and approval controls, but not independent outcomes.

posts.title: Howler: quick AI questions that disappear
posts.promise: Try a macOS menu-bar chat that keeps conversation in memory and burns it when closed.
posts.whatItIs: Howler is a macOS menu-bar app for quick AI questions. Its README says conversation text stays in memory and is removed when the letter is closed; requests go to a model service configured by the user.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a Mac user wanting transient AI chats might pay for this kind of app; the source provides no buyer or pricing evidence.
loop: Install Howler on a supported Mac.
Configure a model service and API key using the app setup.
Open a letter and enter a non-sensitive question.
Review the streamed answer and decide whether to follow it.
Close the letter to burn the conversation.
posts.evidence: The GitHub README documents the macOS app, model configuration, streamed answers, and in-memory conversation behavior.
posts.uncertainty: Project documentation does not establish independent use. Model setup requires a provider and credential. Closing removes conversation text according to the README, but setup and API key remain stored. People should avoid secrets and review answers; the app does not search the web.
first24Hours: Read the README privacy and setup sections.
Try demo mode or configure a model with a non-sensitive question.
Close the letter and confirm its conversation is gone; this would show whether the documented short-chat flow works.

ease.reason: README has setup instructions and demo mode, but model use requires macOS and configuration.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: Mac users may value transient chats; the source gives no buyer, demand, or pricing evidence.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test of a basic question-and-close flow is plausible, though provider setup is an obstacle.

autonomy.reason: Answers stream automatically, but people configure the provider, review responses, and close the chat.

evidence.reason: README documents app behavior and a no-key demo mode, without independent real-use evidence.
